title: Grimnir Attack Playbook
description: A declarative, reachability-aware attack chain. Unlike an execution framework's playbook (which fires modules), a Grimnir playbook is a DECISION recipe: given HUGINN recon signals + the reachability gate taxonomy, it says which specialist to dispatch, what capability each step proves, which confirm-harness artifact validates it, and which never-submit traps the lane risks. Adapted from the Kittysploit playbook model; fitted to Grimnir's delegate-don't-execute design.

id.description: Stable kebab-case identifier, matches the filename stem.

domain.description: Primary domain; drives which specialist leads.

secondary_agents.description: Agents a later step hands off to (e.g. Specter finds SSRF -> Nimbus harvests IMDS creds).

prerequisites.description: When to even consider this playbook. Matched against HUGINN's asset-map.json (technologies, ai_indicators) and intel.jsonl (discovery_type + tags). ANY-of semantics within each list.

signals_any.description: Recon signals: intel discovery_type/tags or asset-map indicators (e.g. graphql, ssrf, webhook, multi_tenant, mcp, imds).

tech_any.description: Case-insensitive substrings matched against asset-map technologies[].name (e.g. wordpress, aws, apollo, grpc).

auth.description: Free-form auth precondition, e.g. 'two isolated tenant accounts, both write-capable'.

reachability.description: The Grimnir-native overlay. Names the gates from the reachability taxonomy that BLOCK this lane if not held; the matcher reads $PROJECT_DIR/reachability.json (gates_held) and annotates the playbook REACHABLE / BLOCKED(gate) / UNKNOWN. Do not plan a primary lane you cannot reach (hunting Rule 1/20-23).

id.description: Step identifier, unique within the playbook.

capability.description: What this step achieves in Grimnir vocabulary (e.g. recon, authz_bypass, ssrf_primitive, deblind, cloud_credentials, data_exfil, prompt_injection, tool_abuse).

action.description: Human-readable description of the test to run.

action_class.description: Phase B action-safety class of this step, driving whether the live-fire lane runner may auto-fire it: read-only | own-account-read (auto-fire, any severity) vs reversible | victim-data-write | destructive (human only). Absence is inferred from the HTTP method. Read by the future lane synthesizer; the executor's gate re-derives it per lane.

confirm.description: Confirm-harness primitive that turns this step from theoretical to confirmed (authz-confirm.py, oob-listener.py, render-confirm.py, mcp-confirm.py, poc-export.py). Absence = no automated proof primitive; validate manually.

evidence_class.description: The scripts/validate-finding.sh --class this step's finding maps to (authz, xss, ssrf, ...). Drives the High/Critical evidence gate.

next_on.description: The step a verdict on this step raises confirmed -> the escalation, candidate -> the step that firms it up. Values are step ids in this chain; the next step is raised for the operator or an agent.

confirm_args.description: Argument template for `confirm`, so `playbook.py plan` can emit a runnable command instead of only naming the primitive. --finding-id and --project-dir are supplied by plan; write only the step-specific arguments here. Use {PLACEHOLDER} for values the operator must fill from the live target (e.g. {TARGET_URL}, {TOKEN_A}, {VICTIM_ID}) -- plan lists them so it is obvious what the step still needs.

blockers.description: Technical barriers that defeat the chain (prose): e.g. 'IMDSv2 with hop limit 1', 'introspection disabled in prod'. Distinct from reachability gates (which are about what the OPERATOR holds).

never_submit.description: never-submit.md triggers this lane risks tripping (e.g. 'blind SSRF with no demonstrable impact', 'CORS without data exposure'). A reminder, not a hard block.

response_channel.description: For lanes whose severity is set by WHAT COMES BACK rather than by the request itself (SSRF above all). A server-side request that fires but returns nothing is the floor of its class; the same request becomes critical when the response is readable. Naming the attainable rungs and the oracle that reads them stops a lane being filed at the floor by default, and stops severity_ceiling being asserted without a channel that could ever justify it.

ladder.description: Rungs this lane can realistically reach, weakest first.

oracle.description: How the response is actually read back: OOB callback only (blind), a delivery log, a rendered screenshot/PDF, an og: metadata field, an error string, a length/timing delta, or a full body reflection.

severity_ceiling.description: Best realistic severity if the terminal step lands. For lanes carrying a response_channel, the ceiling must be justified by the top rung of that ladder -- a blind-only channel caps at medium no matter how good the primitive is.

references.description: Generic references only (OWASP, CVE, hunting-rule numbers). NEVER name a real program, target, or operator artifact — this file is public.
